subject: social_science
title: Causes, Course and Results of World War I
subtitle: Alliances, imperialism, the Sarajevo crisis, global theatres, Treaty of Versailles, and humanitarian impact
curiosity_hook: How did a single assassination in Sarajevo in June 1914 pull empires across Europe, Asia, Africa, and India into four years of global conflict?
learning_objectives: Distinguish long-term structural causes (imperialism, rival alliance blocs, militant nationalism, Balkan instability) from the immediate trigger at Sarajevo (28 June 1914).
Locate major Alliance and Central Powers theatres on an evidence-labelled schematic map without trivializing human suffering.
Explain key provisions of the Treaty of Versailles (28 June 1919), the humanitarian toll, and the social/economic impact on India.

concept_outline.heading: Two Armed Camps & Rival Nationalisms (pp. 4–5)
concept_outline.summary: By 1907, European Great Powers were split into the Triple Alliance (1882: Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy — though Italy later joined the Allies via the 1915 Treaty of London) and the Triple Entente (1907: Britain, France, Russia). Naval arms races, Franco-German hostility over Alsace–Lorraine (1871), and Balkan crises turned Europe into a powder keg.
concept_outline.worked_example: Alliance domino chain (July–August 1914): Sarajevo assassination (28 June) → Austria targets Serbia → Russia mobilizes → Germany declares war on Russia (1 Aug) & crosses neutral Belgium → Britain enters the war.

concept_outline.heading: Industrial & Global Conflict (pp. 5–7)
concept_outline.summary: Fighting spanned the Western Front (Marne 1914, Verdun & Somme 1916, trench warfare), Eastern Front (Tannenberg, Russian Revolution 1917, Brest-Litovsk 3 Mar 1918), Middle East, Africa, and naval theatres (Jutland 1916, cruiser Emden bombarding Madras, unrestricted submarine warfare & Lusitania leading to US entry in April 1917).

concept_outline.heading: Armistice, Treaty of Versailles & Global Impact (pp. 7–9)
concept_outline.summary: Following the 11 November 1918 armistice, the Treaty of Versailles (28 June 1919) imposed war guilt, reparations, army limits (100,000), loss of Alsace–Lorraine & colonies, and established the League of Nations. Eight million soldiers died, three empires collapsed (Germany, Austria-Hungary, Ottoman), and India faced heavy economic strain (£230M cash, £125M loans, £250M materials) alongside the rise of the Home Rule Movement.

key_terms.definition: The two pre-war European alliance camps whose mutual defense pledges escalated a regional Balkan conflict into a world war (p. 4).
Interconnected ditches dug along the Western Front to shelter troops from artillery and machine-gun fire, leading to prolonged stalemate and massive casualties (p. 6).
Peace settlement signed in the Hall of Mirrors imposing reparations, military limits, and territorial losses on Germany (p. 8).
First international collective-security organization proposed in President Wilson's Fourteen Points to prevent future wars (pp. 8, 11).

expected_observations: Historians distinguish underlying structural causes (imperialism, alliances, arms races, nationalism) from the immediate spark at Sarajevo.
The war was truly global — directly affecting colonized societies including India (soldiers, wartime finance, Madras bombardment, and political awakening).
Humanitarian losses (8 million dead, millions wounded, 1918 influenza) and collapsed empires reshaped the 20th-century world map.
limitations: The accompanying SVG map is a schematic educational diagram ('Not to Scale', reflecting 1914–1918 alliance groupings) rather than a precise cartographic border projection.
Historical causes and the fairness of the Treaty of Versailles remain subjects of scholarly interpretation; multiple perspectives are noted.

steps.heading: 1882–1907: Alliance Blocs Harden
steps.description: Triple Alliance (1882: Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy) faced Franco-Russian Alliance (1894), Entente Cordiale (1904), and Triple Entente (1907: Britain, France, Russia).
steps.key_takeaway: Mutual defense commitments meant a local crisis could escalate rapidly.

steps.heading: 1912–1913: Balkan Wars & Rivalries
steps.description: Ottoman retreat sparked the First and Second Balkan Wars (Treaties of London & Bucharest, 1913), sharpening Austro-Serbian hostility.
steps.key_takeaway: The Balkans became the immediate flashpoint of European power politics.

steps.heading: 28 June – August 1914: Sarajevo Crisis & Outbreak
steps.description: Assassination of Archduke Francis Ferdinand in Sarajevo led Austria against Serbia, Germany against Russia & France, and Britain in after Germany violated Belgian neutrality.
steps.key_takeaway: Immediate trigger ignited decades of imperial and nationalist tension.

steps.heading: 1914–1918: Industrial Warfare & Turning Points
steps.description: Trench stalemate on the Western Front (Marne, Verdun, Somme); Russian Revolution (1917) and Brest-Litovsk (Mar 1918); US entry (Apr 1917) after unrestricted submarine warfare.
steps.key_takeaway: First total industrial war affecting civilians, colonies, and global economies.

steps.heading: 11 Nov 1918 & 28 June 1919: Armistice & Treaty of Versailles
steps.description: Germany surrendered Nov 1918; Treaty of Versailles imposed reparations, military caps, and territorial changes, while creating the League of Nations.
steps.key_takeaway: Three empires collapsed, Europe's map was redrawn, and harsh terms left deep tensions.

question_bank.prompt: Which three countries originally formed the Triple Entente by 1907 (History Unit 1, p. 4)?
question_bank.hint: Look at the Entente Cordiale (1904) plus Britain's 1907 agreement.

options.label: Britain, France, and Russia
options.feedback: Correct! Following the Franco-Russian Alliance (1894) and Entente Cordiale (1904), Britain, France, and Russia formed the Triple Entente in 1907.

options.label: Germany, Austria-Hungary, and Italy
options.feedback: Those three nations formed the Triple Alliance in 1882, opposing the Entente.

options.label: Germany, Turkey, and Bulgaria
options.feedback: Germany, Austria-Hungary, Turkey, and Bulgaria fought as the Central Powers during the war.

question_bank.worked_explanation: Social Science p. 4: Triple Alliance (1882) vs Triple Entente (1907: Britain, France, Russia).

question_bank.prompt: What event directly brought Britain into World War I in August 1914 after Germany declared war on Russia and France (p. 5)?
question_bank.hint: Check which neutral country Germany marched through to attack France.

options.label: The German army's violation of Belgian neutrality.
options.feedback: Correct! Germany's invasion of neutral Belgium forced Britain to enter the war on the Allied side.

options.label: The signing of the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk.
options.feedback: The Treaty of Brest-Litovsk was signed much later (3 March 1918) between Russia and Germany.

options.label: The Treaty of Versailles.
options.feedback: The Treaty of Versailles ended the war in June 1919.

question_bank.worked_explanation: Social Science p. 5: 'The German violation of Belgian neutrality forced Britain to enter War.'

question_bank.prompt: Which statement accurately describes the impact of World War I on India according to History Unit 1 (pp. 7–9)?
question_bank.hint: Consider both military/economic contributions and political movements in India.

options.label: Indian soldiers served across three continents, Madras was bombarded by the Emden, India bore heavy wartime expenses and grain distress, and the Home Rule Movement grew.
options.feedback: Spot on! The war deeply affected Indian society, finances (£230M cash, £125M loans, £250M materials), and nationalist politics.

options.label: India was untouched by the war because fighting stayed strictly inside Europe.
options.feedback: WWI was a global conflict — Indian troops served in Europe, Africa, and West Asia, and the German cruiser Emden even bombarded Madras.

options.label: Britain immediately granted full independence to India in 1919.
options.feedback: Although many Indians hoped wartime loyalty would bring self-rule, disappointment followed and intensified the freedom struggle.

question_bank.worked_explanation: Social Science pp. 7–9 detail India's human and financial contributions, economic distress, and the rise of the Home Rule Movement.

question_bank.prompt: Why do historians distinguish long-term causes from the Sarajevo assassination when explaining the outbreak of World War I?
question_bank.hint: Ask whether a single assassination could start a global war without prior tensions.

options.label: Because decades of imperial rivalry, arms races, militant nationalism, and rigid alliances created the volatile conditions that Sarajevo triggered.
options.feedback: Exactly! Distinguishing underlying structural causes from immediate triggers is essential to historical reasoning.

options.label: Because the Sarajevo assassination happened after the war ended.
options.feedback: The assassination happened on 28 June 1914 — one month before war broke out.

options.label: Because European powers had no colonies or alliances before 1914.
options.feedback: Colonial empires and rival alliances had been building across Europe since the late 19th century.

question_bank.worked_explanation: History Unit 1 (pp. 1–5) structures the outbreak into long-term imperialism/alliances/nationalism culminating in the immediate Sarajevo crisis.

worked_feedback: Historians separate structural causes (imperialism, alliances, militarism, nationalism) from immediate catalysts (Sarajevo, 28 June 1914).
Evaluate wars through documented evidence and human/social consequences — never as simplified point-scoring contests.

flashcards.front: What happened on 28 June 1914 and why was it the immediate trigger of WWI?
flashcards.back: Archduke Francis Ferdinand (heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne) was assassinated in Sarajevo, Bosnia, setting off the Austria–Serbia ultimatum and Europe's alliance chain (p. 5).

flashcards.front: Which three major empires collapsed as a direct aftermath of World War I?
flashcards.back: The German Empire, the Austro-Hungarian Empire, and the Ottoman (Turkish) Empire (p. 1).

flashcards.front: When did the Armistice take effect, and when was the Treaty of Versailles signed?
flashcards.back: Armistice: 11 November 1918. Treaty of Versailles: 28 June 1919 in the Hall of Mirrors, Paris (pp. 7–8).

flashcards.front: Why did the United States enter World War I in April 1917 after three years of neutrality?
flashcards.back: Germany declared unrestricted submarine warfare (Jan 1917) and torpedoed ships including the Lusitania, provoking US entry under President Woodrow Wilson (p. 7).
